To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
public communication in crisis is an emerging, important, but largely unexplored area of information science.

(1) the public can be a source of information and a partner in post-impact response, and (2) the information science community can play a significant role in helping formal response organizations better align with the public.

the emerging information pathways of persistent citizen communications are spatially and temporally arranged to serve different functions of post-impact crisis response, but are not well integrated into formal response organizations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
anticipating a future of public participation in crisis response.
how the emerging information environment can be better understood to support the development of more effective response strategies.
how ICT can be used in the post-impact period to support the public's efforts to help themselves and others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of ICT in public participation is not yet fully known and is still in the process of being discovered.
we do not know what will happen, and the only certainty is that the role of ICT in disaster response will continue to evolve.
we are at the beginning of a new era of public participation in crisis response, with ICT as a major enabler.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ICT-supported public participation in crisis is a new, emerging area for research in information science.
we are in the midst of an information science revolution in which the public is becoming an active, information-seeking, information-generating, information-distributing participant.
the public is becoming a more important actor in crisis response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the future of ICT-supported disaster response will require more attention to public participation, and the role ICT can play in enabling it.

information science can contribute to disaster response by anticipating and understanding the emerging forms of public participation, and by supporting the development of appropriate response strategies.

information science researchers need to anticipate the emergence of a future of ICT supported public participation, with implications for disaster response and for information seeking and sharing more broadly.
